opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it helps to separate a few different things that people lump together when they talk about "long context."

The first is just the raw engineering side. With standard attention, the cost grows quadratically with sequence length, and even with all the tricks people have developed, like better kernels, sparse or linear-ish attention variants, and caching, you're still moving a lot of memory around. The KV cache for a very long context gets enormous, and that's a real serving cost. But honestly, I think of that as the more tractable part. It's the kind of problem where you throw good engineers and some compute at it and it keeps getting better. We've seen context windows go from a few thousand tokens to hundreds of thousands and beyond fairly quickly.

The harder and more interesting question is whether the model actually *uses* that context well. You can technically fit a million tokens in, but does the model reason over all of it the way a careful human expert would if they'd read the whole thing? There you see things like the "lost in the middle" phenomenon, where models attend well to the beginning and the end but get fuzzier in between. Retrieval-style tasks, finding a needle in a haystack, turn out to be much easier than tasks where you have to integrate information spread across the whole context and do multi-step reasoning over it.

Part of the reason, I think, is training data. Most natural documents just aren't that long, and even long ones don't have dependencies that genuinely span the whole length. So the model hasn't had much signal teaching it to do really long-range integration. You can construct synthetic data, you can use RL on long tasks, and I think that does help, but it's an area where the data distribution matters as much as the architecture.

Then there's a more conceptual point. I'm not sure the end state is "make the context window infinitely large." Humans don't hold everything in working memory. We have something like a short working context, plus the ability to write things down, look things up, and compress experience into memory. So I suspect a lot of the progress will come from models getting better at managing their own context: summarizing, taking notes, deciding what to retrieve, working over long horizons as agents. Longer raw context helps a lot, but the real goal is long-horizon coherence, and that's partly a capability you train for, not just a window you widen.

So, to sum up: the compute and memory costs are real but I'd bet they keep falling. The deeper obstacle is getting models to reason over long contexts as well as they reason over short ones, and I think that's going to be solved by some mix of scale, better training data and RL, and models learning to manage memory more like people do.

r001.rationale: It describes increasing raw context length as a tractable engineering problem, citing attention costs, memory movement, and rapid context-window growth, while distinguishing that from the harder capability problem of using the context well.

r002.rationale: It says the KV cache for very long contexts gets enormous and identifies it as a real serving cost.

r003.rationale: It discusses weak training signal for long-range integration, but does not say that serving beyond the model’s training context length causes performance degradation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few different layers to this, and people tend to conflate them.

The first layer is just the raw computational one. With standard attention, the cost of processing a sequence scales quadratically with its length. So if you go from, say, 10,000 tokens to a million tokens, you're not paying a hundred times more, you're paying ten thousand times more on the attention part. That's the obstacle people talk about most, and honestly I think it's the least interesting one, because there's been a lot of engineering progress on it. Things like sparse attention, various forms of linear or near-linear attention, sliding windows combined with some global tokens, clever KV cache management. None of these are perfect, but the pure "we can't fit it in memory or afford the FLOPs" problem is more tractable than it looked a few years ago.

The second layer, which I think is the real one, is: does the model actually use the context? You can give a model a million tokens and it will technically "see" all of them, but what you find empirically is that performance degrades in ways that are not just about compute. There's this "lost in the middle" phenomenon where the model attends well to the beginning and the end but kind of loses track of stuff in the middle. And there's a more subtle thing, which is that as the context gets longer, there's more opportunity for distraction. More things that look relevant but aren't. The model's retrieval becomes noisier because the signal it's trying to find is competing with more and more plausible-looking alternatives.

And I think the deep reason for that is a training distribution problem. Most of the data the models learn from is relatively short. There are not that many naturally occurring documents where the thing you need on page 800 depends in a precise way on something that happened on page 12. So the model never really gets strong gradient pressure to build the machinery for very long-range dependencies. You can do synthetic tasks, needle-in-a-haystack type stuff, and the models get good at those, but there's a question of whether that transfers to the messy, real cases, like reasoning over a whole codebase, or tracking the state of a very long agentic task where the model has made a hundred tool calls and has to remember what it concluded in call number seven.

The third layer is something I'd call the coherence or the reasoning problem. It's one thing to retrieve a fact from far back in the context. It's another thing to maintain a consistent model of the world over that whole span. If you're doing a long task, you're not just looking things up, you're integrating. You're updating beliefs. And the architecture doesn't have a natural notion of "here's my current summary of what I know," it has to reconstruct that from the raw context every time. That's an inefficient and somewhat fragile way to do it. Humans don't work that way. We compress, we forget the details and keep the gist, and we have mechanisms for deciding what's worth keeping.

So when people ask me "why don't you just make the context window ten times bigger," my answer is that we can, and we have, and it helps, but the bottleneck gradually moves from "can the model see it" to "can the model think coherently across it." And that second thing I think requires a mix of better training data, better training objectives that actually reward long-range reasoning, and probably some architectural ideas around memory that are less about raw attention over everything and more about what to attend to.

The thing I'd push back on a little is the framing that long context is a separate feature. I actually think it's a window, no pun intended, into general capability. A model that can genuinely reason over a very long span is a model that's better at planning, at agency, at not losing the thread. So in some sense the obstacles to long context are the same as the obstacles to the next level of intelligence, and that's why I find it interesting rather than just an engineering nuisance.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a couple of different problems that get bundled together here. One is just making the computation work. As the context gets longer, the cost of attending to it grows, you have more memory to manage, and you have to figure out how to serve the model efficiently. Those are substantial engineering problems.

But then there’s a separate question: is the model actually using that context? You can put a million tokens into a model, and that doesn’t necessarily mean it can reason effectively about a million tokens.

For example, finding one particular fact in a very long document is a useful test, but it’s a relatively narrow capability. Imagine instead that you need to bring together twenty different pieces of evidence scattered throughout the document, notice that some of them contradict each other, and arrive at a conclusion. That’s a much harder task. You can have good retrieval without having good understanding of the whole thing.

So I would think about the training distribution as well as the architecture. Are you training on tasks where the model actually needs the distant context? If it can get a good training loss by mostly looking at what’s nearby, there isn’t much pressure to learn the harder capability.

My intuition is that this isn’t one fundamental wall. It’s a collection of problems involving compute, training, and evaluation. And the important measure is less ‘How many tokens can I fit?’ and more ‘How much additional useful work can the model do because those tokens are there?’

r003.rationale: It discusses whether training tasks encourage use of distant context, but does not say that serving beyond the trained context length can degrade performance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a few different problems that get bundled together here. One is just computational: as you make the context longer, it becomes more expensive to train on and more expensive to serve. You can make architectural improvements, but you still have to decide how much compute you want to spend on that versus other capabilities.

Then there’s the question of whether the model actually uses the context. Being able to put a million tokens into a model is different from having it reliably notice all the relevant information and reason across it. Finding one fact buried in a long document is a useful test, but it’s a much easier problem than integrating a hundred facts scattered throughout that document.

And I think the training distribution matters a lot. If you want the model to do sophisticated reasoning over long contexts, you need training examples where doing well actually requires that. Otherwise, it can learn to mostly ignore the additional context, or use it in relatively shallow ways.

So I don’t think there’s some obvious fundamental wall. But increasing the number on the context window is only one part of the problem. The harder question is how much useful computation the model can do with everything you’ve put into it.
